name: Wei Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Your name won't go on anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Eastgate Medical Practice, right by the train station and ten minutes from the university, so my patients are students, shift workers and a lot of people who've just moved to the city. Mornings are booked appointments, afternoons are the same-day queue, which is basically whoever got through on the phone at eight. I see about thirty-five people a day: sore throats, contraception, mental health, and the occasional really sick person who thought it was nothing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle, the moment the story clicks and you realise the tiredness is actually the thyroid. What wears me out is chasing things, like a hospital letter that's three weeks late. I'm also the practice's digital lead, which means a small extra allowance and every printer complaint in the building.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a flat with Karim, an old school friend who tests software for a bank. I'm on normal GP pay, I've got about three months of costs saved, and I pay for a climbing gym I use less than I should. No kids, no mortgage, so my costs are pretty light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit of an anticlimax for me. I use AI tools every day, and I'd been expecting more than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I tell the partners now: the note-taker and the letter drafts are worth having, but they're not magic. Online I'd probably post a slightly smug thread about how the hype crowd got it wrong, even though I was half in that crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job is safe and a bit duller than I hoped. My digital lead role would shrink back to fixing printers and running the booking system. I'd miss the feeling of being early to something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, basically. I'd still use the scribe and the letter tool every day, because ten minutes saved a day is fifty minutes a week. And I'd look at a short course in dermatology, something to make the work more interesting, rather than anything to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like turning up to a party that ends at nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were half in the hype crowd. What did you think was going to happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I thought by now AI would be reading every blood result and flagging the odd ones before I'd even opened them. In this picture it does a bit of that, but I'd still be clicking through two hundred normal cholesterol tests a week, and that is not why anyone goes to medical school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any money worries, even in this calmer world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Rent goes up, and I'd like to buy somewhere one day, but GP pay in a city with other practices around is solid. If anything, I'd worry more about my parents' restaurant than about me.

say: The **note-taker** and letter drafts are worth having, but they're **not magic**.
I'd post a slightly smug thread saying the **hype crowd** got it wrong.
think: My job is **safe** and a bit **duller** than I'd hoped.
My **digital lead** role would shrink back to printers and bookings.
do: Keep using the **AI scribe** and letter tool daily, saving about **fifty minutes** a week.
Take a **short dermatology course** to make the work more interesting.
feel: **Calm** but a little **flat**, like a party that ends at nine.
S0.quote: I'd still be clicking through two hundred normal cholesterol tests a week, and that is not why anyone goes to medical school.
fieldNote: His mood dips from **disappointment**, not fear; he wanted more from AI.
He admits he was half in the **hype crowd** he'd mock online.
His only money worry points to his **parents' restaurant**, not his own job.

steps.text: Keep using the AI scribe and letter drafts in every clinic
Sign up for a short dermatology course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I've been half expecting. Writing, checking, booking, answering patients: that's the whole back office of a GP practice and a good chunk of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: this is good news if we do it properly. I'd offer to run the rollout at Eastgate, because someone has to make sure it's tested on our patients and not just in a sales demo. Online I'd write about what actually works and what doesn't, with numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me personally. I'm the one in the building who already knows these tools, so I'd become more useful, not less. The people I'd worry about are the reception and admin team, and maybe the doctors who refuse to touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within the first month I'd put a proposal to the partners: AI triage for the morning phone rush, AI sorting of normal results, and me checking a sample every week to catch errors. I'd also sign up for a part-time certificate in clinical informatics, which is about using computer systems safely in health care. It's about 2,000, and the practice might pay half if I ask nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a little guilt about the admin team. It's like being handed the keys to something I've wanted to fix for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the reception team. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be straight with them, not pretend nothing's changing. Some of them could move into patient support, helping people use the new systems, especially older patients. If AI takes the phones at eight in the morning, someone still has to help the man who can't work the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's good for you. Is there any way it goes badly for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the health board buys some clunky national system and I'm the one blamed for it, yes. Being the AI guy is great until the AI guy is the one patients shout at. But my pay and my job look safe, so I'll take that risk.

say: This is **good news** if we test it on our own patients, not a sales demo.
I'd post **real numbers** online about what works and what doesn't.
think: Knowing the tools already makes me **more useful**, not less.
I'd worry most about the **reception and admin** staff, and doctors who refuse it.
do: Propose **AI triage** for the morning phone rush and AI sorting of normal results.
Check a **weekly sample** of the AI's decisions to catch errors.
Start a part-time **informatics certificate**, about **2,000**, half paid by the practice.
feel: **Excited**, like being handed the keys to something he's wanted to fix.
A little **guilty** about the admin team.
S1.quote: Being the AI guy is great until the AI guy is the one patients shout at.
fieldNote: He sees this world as **his opening**, not a threat.
He's honest that being the **practice's AI guy** carries a risk of blame.
He wants to move reception staff into **patient support**, not just cut them.

steps.text: Propose AI phone triage and results sorting to the Eastgate partners
Check a weekly sample of AI-sorted results for errors
Start the part-time clinical informatics certificate, about 2,000

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's different. That's not a better back office, that's the thing doing my actual job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd try to be useful rather than loud. I'd say doctors need to shape how it's used, because the companies building it won't know what a bad Tuesday in a city practice looks like. I'd be on every panel and committee that would have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the diagnosis bit, the puzzle I said I love, is exactly what goes first. By 2028 it would do it better than me, and certainly better than me at three in the afternoon. What's left for three more years is the hands-on part: examining, injecting, stitching, and being the person who signs. I'm 27, so I'd have a whole career to fill after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd apply for a clinical safety role with the health board, the people who check that these systems don't hurt anyone. I'd keep two or three sessions at Eastgate so I don't lose my hands-on skills. And I'd stop spending on anything big and push my savings from three months to six, because I don't know what the job market for doctors looks like in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. Not helpless, because I'm young, I've got no kids and I can move fast. But the thing I love about the job is the thing that goes first, and that stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you love the puzzle. What happens to that if the machine solves it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I'd have to find a different puzzle. Maybe it's working out why the AI got one case wrong, or why a patient won't take its advice. I spent ten years learning to think like a doctor, and an AI learns it in two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, oddly. Their restaurant is about as hands-on as work gets, and my dad keeps saying there's always a job in the kitchen. I'd laugh, but by 2029 I might be peeling onions on Saturdays.

say: Doctors need to **shape how AI** is used in clinics, not just receive it.
I'd join **every panel** and committee that would have me.
think: The **diagnosis puzzle** I love is exactly what goes first.
I'd have about **three more years** of hands-on work, then a whole career to fill.
do: Apply for a **clinical safety role** with the health board straight away.
Keep **two or three sessions** at Eastgate to hold on to hands-on skills.
Push savings from three months to **six months** of costs.
feel: **Anxious**, though not helpless, because he's young and can move fast.
**Stung** that the part of the job he loves goes first.
S2.quote: I spent ten years learning to think like a doctor, and an AI learns it in two.
fieldNote: Even an early adopter feels this one hits the **core of his job**.
He pivots toward **checking AI safety** rather than competing with it.
His half-joking fallback is his **parents' restaurant** kitchen.

steps.text: Apply for a clinical safety role with the health board
Cut his Eastgate clinics to two or three sessions a week
Build savings from three to six months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a much better runway. I could do a lot in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get organised: train doctors in the tools now, work out the rules now, and not wait for 2031. I'd probably give a talk at the regional GP meeting, because I'd have already been asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to put myself where the work will still be. The boring truth is that I'd be fine for the next three or four years, probably better than fine. It's what happens after 2031 that I can't see clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start a part-time master's in health informatics, about 9,000 over two years, paid partly from savings and partly from extra out-of-hours shifts. I'd keep full clinics at Eastgate while I study. And I'd put about 200 a month into a cheap index fund, because if AI is going to eat everyone's work, I'd rather own a tiny slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, with a bit of excitement. It's like being told the exam date: stressful, but at least you can plan the revision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Extra out-of-hours shifts on top of a master's: how does that work in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two evening shifts a month at the urgent care centre, about 600 extra. It's tiring, but I've done worse in my first hospital job. Karim already complains I'm never home, so he'd barely notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound fairly confident. What would shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the health board decided it didn't need informatics doctors either, because the AI checks itself. Then I'd have spent 9,000 learning to supervise something that doesn't want supervising. I'd still have my hands, though, until about 2034.

say: Now is the time to **train doctors** in the tools and set the **rules**.
I'd give a **talk** at the regional GP meeting about planning ahead.
think: Five years is enough to **put myself** where the work will still be.
The next **three or four years** look fine; after 2031 I can't see clearly.
do: Start a **part-time master's** in health informatics, about **9,000** over two years.
Work **two out-of-hours shifts** a month for about 600 extra.
Put about **200 a month** into a cheap index fund.
feel: **Uneasy**, with some **excitement**, like being told the exam date.
S3.quote: If AI is going to eat everyone's work, I'd rather own a tiny slice of it.
fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a **study plan** with costs attached.
He wants to **own a slice** of AI rather than only compete with it.
His doubt is whether the health board will need **AI supervisors** for long.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time health informatics master's, about 9,000
Work two urgent care evening shifts a month for 600
Put 200 a month into a low-cost index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to almost forget about it, which is its own danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we have no excuse. Ten years is two rounds of training for new family doctors, so medical schools should be changing what they teach right now. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, and some who wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm. I'd be 37 when it lands, with ten years of experience in both medicine and the tech side. I think I'd end up running how AI is used across a group of practices, or doing something that doesn't exist yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year looks a lot like the slow picture: keep using the tools every day, keep full clinics, start the informatics certificate. I'd put a bit into an index fund, maybe 150 a month. And I'd start saving for a flat properly, because a ten-year runway is long enough for a mortgage to make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small itch. The itch is that ten years makes people lazy, and I don't want to be the one who wakes up in 2035 having done nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone around you worry you about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim, actually. He tests software for a bank, so his work goes in 2036 just like the diagnosis part of mine, but he'd shrug and say it's ages away. I'd probably nag him into a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a student starting medical school now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a medical student to become very good with their hands and very good with people, because those are the last two things the machines learn. And to learn how the AI thinks, so they can tell when it's wrong.

say: With ten years, we have **no excuse** not to prepare.
**Medical schools** should be changing what they teach right now.
think: I'd be **37**, with experience in both medicine and **the tech side**.
I could end up **running AI use** across a group of practices.
do: Start the **informatics certificate** while keeping full clinics.
Put about **150 a month** into an index fund.
Start saving for a **flat deposit**, since a mortgage now makes sense.
feel: **Calm**, with an itch that ten years makes people **lazy**.
S4.quote: I'd tell a medical student to become very good with their hands and very good with people, because those are the last two things the machines learn.
fieldNote: He fears **complacency** more than the technology itself.
He worries about his **flatmate's job** more than his own.
His advice to students is **hands and people**, plus knowing when AI is wrong.

steps.text: Start the clinical informatics certificate in the first year
Put 150 a month into a low-cost index fund
Start saving properly for a flat deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd starve, but because the part of medicine I love goes first and there's no time to build the next thing. What would help is the health board creating proper roles for doctors to check and run these systems, paid like clinical work, not squeezed in on a Friday afternoon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what patients would choose. A lot of my student patients would happily see an AI at midnight rather than wait three days for a doctor. A GP who pretends that won't happen is in for a nasty surprise.

headlineQuote: A lot of my student patients would happily see an AI at midnight rather than wait three days for a doctor.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old GP** at a city practice near the station, serving students and shift workers.
He is the practice's **digital lead** and uses AI tools every day.
He welcomes slow change as **his opening**, but fast AGI takes the diagnosis work he loves.
His plans run through **informatics study**, clinical safety roles and a small index fund.
Single and **renting with a friend**, he has light costs and room to move fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the part of medicine he loves goes first with no time to build the next thing.
whatWouldHelp: **Proper paid roles** for doctors to check and run AI systems, not Friday-afternoon extras.
